title: Find Left Most and Right Most Index of Element
description: Given a sorted array A of size N and an integer B, return [firstIndex(B), lastIndex(B)]. If B is absent return [-1, -1]. Must be O(log N).
story: Two binary searches, same shape. Once you hit the target, don't celebrate — keep walking left to find the first occurrence, then run a second BS walking right to find the last.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: scan left → right, record first and last index where A[i] == B
solutions.story: If you're allowed a single linear pass, this is the lazy answer. Two pointers — first hit goes to 'first', every hit overwrites 'last'.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
BS1 → on hit: store first, high = mid - 1
BS2 → on hit: store last,  low  = mid + 1
solutions.story: Same loop body twice, only the 'on equal' branch flips direction. Memorise: 'first hugs left, last hugs right.'

data.footer: Two-phase binary search — A = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], B = 8. First BS finds leftmost 8, second finds rightmost.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Sorted array A = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], target B = 8. Find first and last indices where A[i] == 8. Strategy: run two independent binary searches. Phase 1 finds the leftmost occurrence, Phase 2 finds the rightmost.
script.overlay: Twin BS pattern: first hugs left (high = mid - 1 on match), last hugs right (low = mid + 1 on match). Both searches have identical loop structure, only the 'on equal' branch flips.

script.label: PHASE 1 — INITIALISE (find first)
script.msg: Phase 1 start: low = 0, high = 5, first = -1. Search the full array [0..5] for the first occurrence of 8. When we hit a match, we'll store it but keep searching left to see if an earlier match exists.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 1 (mid=2)
script.msg: mid = (0+5)/2 = 2. Check A[2] = 7. Since 7 < 8, the target must be to the right of mid. Eliminate left half [0..2] → low = mid + 1 = 3.
script.overlay: Standard BS: A[mid] < B → discard left → low = mid + 1.

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 2 (mid=4, first match)
script.msg: mid = (3+5)/2 = 4. Check A[4] = 8. Perfect match! 8 == 8 ✓. Store first = 4 as a candidate. But there might be an earlier occurrence of 8 to the left → push high = mid - 1 = 3 and continue searching.
script.overlay: Lower-bound BS: on match, store the candidate but keep searching left: first = mid; high = mid - 1;

script.label: PHASE 1 — Iteration 3 (mid=3, better match)
script.msg: mid = 3. Check A[3] = 8. Another match! 8 == 8 ✓. Update first = 3 (this is earlier than index 4). Push high = mid - 1 = 2. Now low = 3 > high = 2 → Phase 1 terminates. First occurrence locked at index 3.

script.label: PHASE 2 — INITIALISE (find last)
script.msg: Phase 2 start: Reset search window. Now hunt for the last occurrence of 8. low = 0, high = 5, last = -1. This time, when we match, we push low right instead of high left.
script.overlay: Upper-bound BS: on match, store the candidate but keep searching right: last = mid; low = mid + 1;

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 1 (mid=2)
script.msg: mid = 2. Check A[2] = 7 < 8. The target lies to the right → eliminate [0..2], set low = 3.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 2 (mid=4, match)
script.msg: mid = 4. Check A[4] = 8. Match! 8 == 8 ✓. Store last = 4 and search right for a later occurrence → low = mid + 1 = 5.

script.label: PHASE 2 — Iteration 3 (mid=5)
script.msg: mid = 5. Check A[5] = 10 > 8. The target is to the left → high = mid - 1 = 4. Now low = 5 > high = 4 → Phase 2 terminates. Last occurrence locked at index 4.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = [3, 4]. First occurrence of 8 is at index 3, last occurrence at index 4. Two O(log N) binary searches — total 6 probes for N=6. Linear scan would need up to 6 comparisons.
script.overlay: Core pattern: same BS loop body twice. Only difference: first search narrows from the right on match, last search narrows from the left. Memorize: first hugs left, last hugs right.

title: Search Insert Position (Lower Bound)
description: Sorted A, target B. If B exists return its index, else return the index of the smallest element ≥ B (or N if all are smaller).
story: This IS lower_bound dressed in interview clothes. Keep an ans = N sentinel — it auto-handles the 'insert at end' case.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: scan i = 0..N-1; first i with A[i] >= B is the answer; else N
solutions.story: Walk until something is at least as big as B. If nothing is, you append.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
ans = N
while low <= high:
  if A[mid] < B  → low = mid + 1
  else           → ans = mid, high = mid - 1
return ans
solutions.story: Whenever you find something ≥ B, lock it in as a candidate and keep looking left for an earlier one. The sentinel N is your safety net.

data.footer: Lower bound binary search — A = [1,3,5,6], B = 5. Find index where B exists or should be inserted.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Sorted array A = [1, 3, 5, 6], target B = 5. Find the index where B exists, or where it should be inserted to keep the array sorted. This is lower_bound — the first position where an element ≥ B can be found or placed.
script.overlay: Core strategy: maintain ans = N (sentinel — one past the end). When A[mid] ≥ B, record ans = mid and search left: high = mid - 1. Sentinel auto-handles the 'insert at end' case.

script.label: INITIALISE
script.msg: Set low = 0, high = 3, ans = N = 4 (the sentinel). If no element ≥ 5 exists in the array, we'll return 4, meaning 'insert after index 3 (at the end)'. Search window covers all 4 elements.

script.label: ITERATION 1 — mid=1 (too small)
script.msg: mid = (0+3)/2 = 1. Check A[1] = 3. Is 3 < 5? Yes! This means the target (or its insertion slot) must be to the right of mid. Discard the left half [0..1] → low = mid + 1 = 2.
script.overlay: BS direction rule: A[mid] < B → answer cannot be in [low..mid] → low = mid + 1.

script.label: ITERATION 2 — mid=2 (exact match)
script.msg: mid = (2+3)/2 = 2. Check A[2] = 5. Perfect match! 5 == 5 ✓. This is a valid answer. Store ans = 2. But for lower_bound, we must confirm this is the first occurrence of 5, so search left: high = mid - 1 = 1.
script.overlay: Lower_bound on exact match: store the index, but keep searching left to ensure it's the leftmost: ans = mid; high = mid - 1;

script.label: ITERATION 3 — loop terminates
script.msg: Now low = 2 > high = 1 → binary search terminates. The stored ans = 2 is the first position where an element ≥ 5 exists. Since A[2] = 5, the element is present at index 2.

script.label: EDGE CASE 1 — absent value (B=4)
script.msg: What if B = 4 (not in array)? Same algorithm: A[1]=3 < 4 → low=2. A[2]=5 > 4 → 5 ≥ 4 ✓ → store ans=2, high=1. Loop exits. Return 2 → insert 4 before 5 to maintain sorted order.
script.overlay: Lower_bound guarantees: if B present → its index; if B absent → the insertion point that keeps array sorted.

script.label: EDGE CASE 2 — larger than all (B=7)
script.msg: What if B = 7 (larger than all elements)? A[2]=5 < 7 → low=3. A[3]=6 < 7 → low=4 > high=3. Loop exits. We never stored ans → sentinel ans = 4 is returned. Insert 7 at the end (index 4).
script.overlay: Sentinel N elegantly handles the 'larger than all' case with zero special-case code. It's already the correct answer.

script.label: EDGE CASE 3 — smaller than all (B=0)
script.msg: What if B = 0 (smaller than all)? A[1]=3 > 0 → 3 ≥ 0 ✓ → store ans=1, high=0. A[0]=1 > 0 → store ans=0, high=-1. Loop exits. Return 0 → insert at the beginning.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 2 for B=5. Target exists at index 2. Binary search took 2 interior probes for N=4, vs up to 4 comparisons for linear scan. Lower_bound is the workhorse of sorted-array algorithms: range queries, merge operations, and duplicate handling all build on this pattern.
script.overlay: Three cases, one algorithm: (1) target present → returns its index. (2) target absent → returns insertion point. (3) target larger than all → sentinel N handles it. No if-else, just one clean loop.

title: Single Element in Sorted Array
description: Every element appears twice in sorted order, except one unique element. Find it in O(log N).
story: Before the unique element, pairs sit at (even, odd). After it, they shift to (odd, even). Binary search hunts for where the pattern breaks.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode:
for i in 0..N-1 step 2: if A[i] != A[i+1] return A[i]
return A[N-1]
solutions.story: Walk in twos. The first time the pair breaks, the left side is your loner.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.story: Even index + matches its neighbour = the loner is past you. Odd index + matches = the loner is behind you. Walk by 2, never by 1.

solutions.label: Alternative — XOR
solutions.pseudocode: xor all elements; pairs cancel; what's left is the loner
solutions.story: If you forget the index-parity trick, XOR every element. Duplicates annihilate, the lone one survives. Not O(log) but bulletproof.

data.footer: Index-parity binary search — A = [1,1,2,2,3,3,4,5,5]. Every element appears twice except one. Use parity to guide BS direction.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Sorted array A = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5] of length N = 9. Every element appears exactly twice, except one unique element. Constraint: sorted order and all duplicates are adjacent. The unique element breaks the pair pattern. Key insight: before the unique, pairs sit at (even, odd) indices; after it, they shift to (odd, even).
script.overlay: Core strategy: at each mid, check if A[mid] matches its neighbor. Combine this with mid % 2 (parity check) to determine which side the unique element is on. If mid is even and matches A[mid+1] → pattern intact on left → unique is after. If mid is odd and matches A[mid+1] → pattern broken on left → unique is before.

script.label: CHECK BOUNDARIES
script.msg: Before binary searching the interior, check both edges. Left edge: A[0]=1 vs A[1]=1 → they match ✓, so index 0 is not the loner. Right edge: A[8]=5 vs A[7]=5 → they match ✓, so index 8 is not the loner. Both boundaries are paired → the unique element lies in the interior [1..7].
script.overlay: Edge case handling: if (A[0] != A[1]) return A[0]; and if (A[N-1] != A[N-2]) return A[N-1]; → if either boundary is unpaired, it's the answer. Otherwise, search the safe interior.

script.label: INITIALISE
script.msg: Set low = 1, high = 7. Binary search the interior [1..7], using index parity + neighbor matching to guide direction. We'll never touch out-of-bounds neighbors.

script.label: ITERATION 1 — mid=4 (even, match right)
script.msg: mid = (1+7)/2 = 4 (even index). Check A[4] = 3 against neighbors. A[3] = 2 (no match), A[5] = 3 (match ✓). Since mid is even and matches its right neighbor, the pair (4,5) is intact. Pattern is unbroken before mid → the unique element must be after index 5. Skip the pair: low = mid + 2 = 6.
script.overlay: Parity rule: mid % 2 == 0 && A[mid] == A[mid+1] → left pattern intact → unique is on the right → low = mid + 2 (skip the matched pair).

script.label: ITERATION 2 — mid=6 (even, no match)
script.msg: mid = 6. Check A[6] = 4 against neighbors. A[5] = 3 (no match), A[7] = 5 (no match). A[6] matches neither neighbor! This means A[6] = 4 is the unique element. The pair pattern is broken at index 6. Return 4.
script.overlay: Base case: when A[mid] != A[mid-1] AND A[mid] != A[mid+1], mid is the loner. This is the termination condition — no parity check needed.

script.label: PATTERN VISUALISATION — before unique
script.msg: Pair indices before the unique: [1,1] at (even=0, odd=1), [2,2] at (even=2, odd=3), [3,3] at (even=4, odd=5). Pattern: first element of pair at even index. Unique at 6. Pairs after: [5,5] at (odd=7, even=8). Pattern flips!
script.overlay: Why parity works: before unique, pairs start at even indices. After unique, pairs start at odd indices. The unique element shifts all subsequent pairs by 1.

script.label: ALTERNATIVE — XOR scan (O(N))
script.msg: Alternative approach: XOR all elements. 1⊕1⊕2⊕2⊕3⊕3⊕4⊕5⊕5 = 4. Duplicate pairs cancel out (x⊕x=0), leaving only the unique element. Simpler code but O(N), not O(log N). When to use: (1) array not sorted, (2) debugging, (3) coding interview time pressure.
script.overlay: XOR trick: int x = 0; for(int v : A) x ^= v; return x; → bulletproof but linear. Parity BS is faster but requires sorted duplicates.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 4 at index 6. The index-parity binary search visited only 2 interior probes for N=9, avoiding a full linear scan. Complexity: O(log N) time, O(1) space. This pattern appears in: 'Single Element in Sorted Array' (LeetCode 540), 'Find Peak Element' variants, and any problem exploiting positional invariants.
script.overlay: Core takeaway: when a sorted array has a structural pattern (here: pairs), and an anomaly breaks that pattern in a monotonic way, you can binary search by checking the pattern's integrity at mid, rather than comparing values directly. The unique element acts as a 'fault line' — everything on one side follows the old pattern, everything on the other follows the new pattern.

title: Find a Peak Element
description: Find any element ≥ both neighbours. Corners count if they beat their one neighbour. Guaranteed a single peak. Solve in O(log N).
story: If you're standing on a slope, walk uphill. That direction must contain a peak. Binary search just walks uphill twice as fast.
plain: You're standing somewhere on the array. Look at the value to your left and the value to your right. Whichever side goes UP — walk that way. Keep doing this and you must reach a peak, because the array can't climb forever. Binary search lets you take giant uphill steps instead of one-by-one.
tale: A blindfolded hiker is dropped onto a strange mountain. He cannot see the summit. But at every step, his fingertips can feel whether the slope tilts up or down beside his feet. So he makes a vow: 'I will always step toward the rising ground.' The mountain is mischievous — it has hidden valleys and false flats — but it has exactly one peak. As long as the hiker keeps choosing the rising side, the mountain itself is funnelling him to the summit. He doesn't need to see. He just needs to trust the slope.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.plain: Walk the array from left to right. At every index, check whether both neighbours are smaller. The first such element is a peak. Handle the two corners separately (they have only one neighbour).
solutions.tale: A patient watchman walks the whole ridge from sunrise. He stops at every rock and looks both ways. The moment he finds a rock taller than its two neighbours, he plants his flag and goes home.
approach: If N == 1, the only element is the peak.
Check the left corner: if A[0] >= A[1], return A[0].
Check the right corner: if A[N-1] >= A[N-2], return A[N-1].
Loop i from 1 to N-2 and return the first A[i] that is >= both A[i-1] and A[i+1].
solutions.pseudocode: scan; return A[i] when both neighbours are smaller
solutions.story: Just look. Linear and obvious.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use binary search. At the midpoint, compare with both neighbours. If mid beats both, you found a peak. Otherwise look at the slope: if A[mid] > A[mid-1] you're climbing, so a peak must lie to the right — throw away the left half. Otherwise throw away the right half. Repeat until you land on the peak.
solutions.tale: The blindfolded hiker grows impatient. Instead of one step at a time, he teleports to the middle of the unexplored stretch and feels the slope. If it rises, he abandons everything behind him — the peak cannot be in flat or downhill territory. If it falls, he abandons everything ahead. Half the mountain disappears with each teleport. In a handful of jumps, he is standing on the summit.
approach: Handle N == 1 and both corner cases up front so the loop never touches an out-of-bound neighbour.
Set low = 1, high = N - 2 (the safe interior range).
While low <= high, compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
If A[mid] is greater than both A[mid-1] and A[mid+1], return A[mid] — you are on the peak.
Else if A[mid] > A[mid-1], the slope rises to the right, so push low = mid + 1.
Otherwise the slope falls, so a peak must be on the left: high = mid - 1.
solutions.pseudocode:
Pre-check both boundaries.
Loop low=1, high=N-2:
  if A[mid] beats both neighbours → return A[mid]
  else if A[mid] > A[mid-1]      → climbing, go right
  else                            → descending, go left
solutions.story: Don't think 'find target'. Think 'walk toward higher ground'. A peak must exist in the direction of increase.

data.footer: Hand-authored walkthrough — A = [5, 17, 100, 11]. Algorithm: O(log N) peak BS.

script.label: Setup
script.msg: Array A = [5, 17, 100, 11]. A peak is any element ≥ both its neighbours. Corners count if they beat their one neighbour. We'll first rule out the two corners, then binary-search the interior.

script.label: Corner check ⓛ — left edge
script.msg: Look at the left corner: A[0]=5 vs A[1]=17. Is 5 ≥ 17? No — the slope rises away from index 0, so it cannot be a peak.
script.overlay: Rule: A[0] >= A[1] ? If yes → return A[0]. Here 5 < 17, so skip.

script.label: Corner check ② — right edge
script.msg: Look at the right corner: A[3]=11 vs A[2]=100. Is 11 ≥ 100? No — the slope rises away from index 3 too.
script.overlay: Rule: A[N-1] >= A[N-2] ? Here 11 < 100, so skip. Both corners ruled out → enter interior BS.

script.label: Initialise interior search
script.msg: Interior range: low = 1, high = N-2 = 2. Search window is just indices 1 and 2. Both corners are now permanently eliminated.
script.overlay: Why low=1, high=N-2? So mid-1 and mid+1 are always safe — no out-of-bounds neighbour.

script.label: Iteration 1 — pick mid
script.msg: mid = 1 + (2-1)/2 = 1. Inspect A[1] = 17 and its neighbours A[0]=5, A[2]=100.

script.label: Iteration 1 — compare neighbours
script.msg: Is A[1]=17 greater than both neighbours? A[0]=5 ✓ but A[2]=100 ✗. Not a peak. Check the slope direction: A[1]=17 vs A[mid-1]=A[0]=5. 17 > 5 → we are climbing rightward.
script.overlay: Decision: slope climbs right → a peak must lie to the right → set low = mid + 1 = 2.

script.label: Iteration 2 — window shrinks
script.msg: low = 2, high = 2. Only one cell left in the interior. mid = 2. Inspect A[2] = 100.

script.label: Iteration 2 — peak found
script.msg: A[2]=100 vs A[1]=17 and A[3]=11. 100 > 17 ✓ and 100 > 11 ✓ — beats both neighbours. Return 100.
script.overlay: Trace summary: corners skipped → 1 BS iteration narrowed to index 2 → peak. Visited 2 interior probes for N=4, vs 4 for brute scan.

script.label: Done
script.msg: ✅ Answer = 100 at index 2. The hiker took giant uphill jumps — at every probe he asked only one question: which side rises? — and the mountain funnelled him to the summit in O(log N).

title: Minimum Difference
description: Matrix C of A×B. For each adjacent row pair, find the minimum absolute difference between any element of row i and any element of row i+1. Return the smallest such diff.
story: Sort each row, then for every element pick its closest neighbour in the next row using lower_bound. Track the smallest |diff| globally.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
sort each row
for each i, j:
  lb = lower_bound(C[i+1], C[i][j])
  consider |C[i][j] - C[i+1][lb]|     (closest greater)
  consider |C[i][j] - C[i+1][lb-1]|   (closest smaller)
  update ans = min
solutions.story: Closest = one of two: the first element ≥ you, or the one right before it. Lower bound gives you both for free.

title: Maximum Height of Staircase
description: Given A blocks, build max-height staircase where stair i needs i blocks. Find max h such that 1+2+...+h ≤ A.
story: h·(h+1)/2 ≤ A. Either solve the quadratic, binary search on h, or just walk one stair at a time. All three work.

solutions.label: Brute (greedy walk)
solutions.pseudocode:
x = 1, steps = 0
while A >= x: A -= x; steps++; x++
return steps
solutions.story: Just keep buying the next stair until you can't afford it. Surprisingly fast — only ~√(2A) stairs exist.

solutions.label: Optimal (BS on answer)
solutions.pseudocode: low=0, high=sqrt(2A)+1; find max h with h*(h+1)/2 <= A
solutions.story: Classic BS on answer. Predicate is monotonic — once h is too tall, every larger h is also too tall.

title: Square Root of Integer
description: Compute floor(sqrt(A)) without using Math.sqrt. A up to 1e9 means mid*mid overflows int — use long.
story: Largest x with x·x ≤ A. Standard BS on answer. The only trap is integer overflow when squaring mid.

solutions.pseudocode: for x = 0..: if x*x > A return x - 1
solutions.story: Linear scan until you overshoot.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode: low=1, high=A/2; track largest mid with mid*mid <= A (as long)
solutions.story: Use long for the multiplication. A/2 is a sharper upper bound than A.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Given A = 11, compute floor(√11) without using Math.sqrt. Find the largest integer x such that x² ≤ 11. This is a classic binary search on answer problem. The search space is [0..A], but we can tighten it: for any x > A/2, we have x² > A (except x=1), so high = A/2 is a sharp upper bound.

Goal: find floor(√11) = largest integer x with x² ≤ 11
script.overlay: Predicate: mid * mid <= A ? If yes, mid is feasible (store as candidate). If no, mid is too large. Critical: Use long for the multiplication mid*mid to avoid integer overflow when A is large (up to 10⁹).

script.label: OVERFLOW TRAP — why long?
script.msg: Consider A = 2×10⁹. The answer is around √(2×10⁹) ≈ 44721. During BS, mid could be around 10⁵. If we compute (int) mid * mid, the product is 10¹⁰, which overflows a 32-bit int (max ≈ 2.1×10⁹). The result wraps around to a negative number or garbage → BS fails. Solution: cast to long before squaring: long sq = (long)mid * mid;. Long is 64-bit, max ≈ 9×10¹⁸.
script.overlay: Overflow formula: int max ≈ 2×10⁹ → sqrt(max) ≈ 46340. Any mid > 46340 will overflow when squared as int. Since A can be 10⁹, we must use long.

title: Rotated Sorted Array Search
description: Sorted array rotated at unknown pivot. Find target index in O(log N). No duplicates.
story: First find the rotation pivot with BS (smallest element). Then you know which sorted half contains B and run a normal BS on that half.

solutions.label: Brute
solutions.pseudocode: linear scan
solutions.story: If it's small, scan it. Otherwise it's a sin.

solutions.label: Optimal — pivot + BS
solutions.pseudocode:
k = rotationFactor(A)   // index of smallest element
if B == A[0] return 0
if B > A[0] → search [0, k-1]
else        → search [k, N-1]
solutions.story: Pivot splits the array into two sorted halves. A[0] tells you which half B lives in. Then it's vanilla BS.

data.footer: Rotated sorted array search — A = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], B = 0. Detect sorted half at each step, check if target lies in it.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Array A = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target B = 0. This was originally a sorted array [0,1,2,4,5,6,7], then rotated at an unknown pivot. The pivot is at index 4 (element 0 is the smallest). Key insight: although the full array is not sorted, at least one half around any mid is sorted. Strategy: at each BS step, identify which half is sorted, check if target lies in that sorted half's range, then decide direction.
script.overlay: Core pattern: at each mid, compare A[mid] with A[low]. If A[low] ≤ A[mid], the left half [low..mid] is sorted (monotonic). Otherwise, the right half [mid..high] is sorted. Once you know which half is sorted, use the standard range-check: is B in [A[low]..A[mid]] or [A[mid]..A[high]]? Decide direction accordingly.

script.label: INITIALISE
script.msg: Set low = 0, high = 6. Binary search the full array [0..6] for target B = 0. At each step, we'll detect the sorted half, check if B is in it, and narrow the window.

script.label: ITERATION 1 — mid=3, left half sorted
script.msg: mid = (0+6)/2 = 3. Check which half is sorted: compare A[low]=4 vs A[mid]=7. Is 4 ≤ 7? Yes ✓ → the left half [4,5,6,7] is sorted. Now check: is target B=0 in the range [A[low]..A[mid]] = [4..7]? No (0 < 4). The target is not in the sorted left half. Discard left half → low = mid + 1 = 4.
script.overlay: Decision tree: (1) Identify sorted half: A[low] ≤ A[mid] → left is sorted. (2) Check if B ∈ [A[low]..A[mid]]: A[low] ≤ B ≤ A[mid]? (3) If yes → search left (high = mid - 1). If no → search right (low = mid + 1).

script.label: ITERATION 2 — mid=5, left half sorted
script.msg: mid = (4+6)/2 = 5. Check which half is sorted: A[low]=0 vs A[mid]=1. Is 0 ≤ 1? Yes ✓ → the left half [0,1] is sorted. Check: is target B=0 in [A[low]..A[mid]] = [0..1]? Yes! (0 is the left boundary). The target is in the sorted left half. Discard right half → high = mid - 1 = 4.
script.overlay: Key: we check the sorted half first because we can use standard range logic there. The unsorted half may have a rotation pivot, making range checks unreliable.

script.label: ITERATION 3 — mid=4 (match!)
script.msg: mid = 4. Check A[4] = 0. Does 0 == B=0? Yes ✓! Perfect match. Return index 4.
script.overlay: Base case: whenever A[mid] == B, return mid immediately. No further probes needed.

script.label: SORTED HALF DETECTION — why it works
script.msg: A rotated sorted array is actually two sorted subarrays concatenated: [4,5,6,7] (ascending) + [0,1,2] (ascending). The rotation pivot separates them. At any mid, at least one of [low..mid] or [mid..high] is entirely within one subarray → that half is sorted. We detect it by comparing A[low] vs A[mid]. Once detected, we can use standard binary search logic on that half: check if B is in [A[sorted_left]..A[sorted_right]].
script.overlay: Why guaranteed? The pivot splits the array into two monotonic chunks. Any [low..mid] or [mid..high] window either (1) lies entirely within one chunk → sorted, or (2) spans the pivot → the other half doesn't span it, so it's sorted. At least one half is always clean.

script.label: RIGHT HALF SORTED — example (mid=2)
script.msg: What if mid was 2? A[low]=4, A[mid]=6. Is 4 ≤ 6? Yes → left half [4,5,6] sorted. But suppose A[low]=6, A[mid]=0 (different rotation). Is 6 ≤ 0? No → left half is not sorted → the right half must be sorted. Then check if B is in [A[mid]..A[high]] and decide.
script.overlay: Decision logic for right-sorted: if A[mid] ≤ B ≤ A[high], search right (low = mid + 1). Else search left (high = mid - 1).

script.label: EDGE CASE — no rotation (already sorted)
script.msg: What if the array is not rotated at all? E.g., [0,1,2,4,5,6,7]. Then A[low] ≤ A[mid] is always true (left half always sorted), and standard BS works. The algorithm degenerates to vanilla binary search. The rotation-detection logic is backward-compatible with sorted arrays.
script.overlay: Rotation count = 0 → A[0] < A[N-1]. The 'sorted half' is always the left half at every step. The algorithm still works.

script.label: EDGE CASE — target not in array
script.msg: What if B = 10 (not in array)? Same algorithm: at each step, detect sorted half, check range, narrow. Eventually low > high without finding a match → return -1. The termination condition is the same as vanilla BS.

script.label: DONE
script.msg: ✅ Answer = index 4 (value 0). At each of 3 iterations, we detected the sorted half by comparing A[low] vs A[mid], checked if B was in the sorted range, and decided direction. Binary search on a rotated array: O(log N), same as vanilla BS. No need to find the pivot first — the algorithm handles the rotation implicitly. Complexity: O(log N) time, O(1) space. This pattern appears in: 'Search in Rotated Sorted Array' (LeetCode 33), 'Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array' (LeetCode 153), 'Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (with duplicates)' (LeetCode 81).
script.overlay: Core takeaway: when a sorted structure is rotated (or cyclically shifted), you can still binary search by exploiting the fact that at least one half is always sorted. The key skill is detecting which half is clean, then applying standard range logic to it. Memorise: if (A[low] <= A[mid]) { /* left sorted, check if B in [A[low]..A[mid]] */ } else { /* right sorted, check if B in [A[mid]..A[high]] */ }. This pattern extends to finding the minimum, the rotation count, and search-with-duplicates (with a degeneracy case).

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: Two sorted arrays A, B. Return the median of the merged sequence. Must run in O(log(min(M,N))).
story: Don't merge. Binary search a partition on the smaller array such that everything on the left of both arrays ≤ everything on the right. The median falls out of the four boundary values.

solutions.label: Brute — merge and pick
solutions.pseudocode: merge using two pointers; return middle (or avg of middle two)
solutions.story: Easy and correct but doesn't meet the log requirement.

solutions.label: Optimal — BS on partition
solutions.pseudocode:
Ensure A is the smaller array.
low=0, high=|A|; leftCount = (M+N+1)/2
Loop:
  pX = (low+high)/2; pY = leftCount - pX
  4 boundary values (use ±∞ at edges)
  if maxLeftX <= minRightY && maxLeftY <= minRightX: done
  else if maxLeftX > minRightY: high = pX - 1
  else: low = pX + 1
solutions.story: Slice both arrays into 'left' and 'right' halves. Valid slice = each side's max ≤ the other side's min. Median pops out of the four corner values.

title: Aggressive Cows
description: Place B cows in N stalls (positions in A). Maximize the minimum distance between any two placed cows.
story: Binary search the minimum distance. For each guess d, greedily place cows: first at A[0], each next at first stall ≥ lastPlaced + d. If B cows fit, try larger d.
plain: You have a row of stalls along a line and a herd of angry cows. You want every pair of cows to be as far apart as possible — specifically, you want the SMALLEST gap to be as big as you can make it. Guess a gap d. Walk the stalls left to right placing a cow each time you've travelled at least d from the last cow. If you can fit all B cows, the gap is achievable — try a bigger one. If not, shrink it. Binary search finds the largest d that still works.
tale: In a long stable, a farmer keeps B cows who despise each other. Put any two close and they kick the wood until it splinters. The farmer has stalls at uneven positions and one question: how far apart can I FORCE them to be, in the worst pair? He plays a game with himself. 'Could I keep them 13 paces apart?' He walks the stalls, dropping a cow only when 13 paces have passed since the last. If all B cows find a home, he smiles — maybe 14 would work too. If they don't fit, he tries 12. The farmer is doing binary search on the cows' patience.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Sort the stall positions. The answer lies somewhere between 1 and (last - first). Binary search this range. For each midpoint d, run a greedy check: place the first cow at stalls[0], then each next cow at the first stall whose position is at least d away from the last placed cow. Count how many cows you placed. If that count >= B, d is feasible — record it and push low up. Otherwise pull high down.
solutions.tale: The farmer sorts the stalls by position so his walk is one straight march. He picks a candidate distance, tries it once with a greedy hand — first cow at stall one, then skip ahead until the wood is far enough away, then drop the next — and counts. If all his cows found peace, he raises his ambition. If not, he lowers it. Each round halves the uncertainty until only one answer remains.
approach: Sort the stall array A so positions are monotonic.
Set low = 1, high = A[N-1] - A[0] — the search space for the minimum distance.
While low <= high, take mid = (low + high) / 2 as the candidate gap d.
Run canPlace(d): start with one cow placed at A[0] and lastPlaced = A[0]. Walk i = 1..N-1; whenever A[i] - lastPlaced >= d, place a cow there and update lastPlaced.
If the placed count reaches B, the gap d works — store result = mid and push low = mid + 1 to chase a bigger gap.
Otherwise the gap is too greedy — pull high = mid - 1 and try again.
When low > high, result holds the maximum minimum distance.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort A
low = 1, high = A[N-1] - A[0]
mid = candidate distance
if canPlace(mid): ans = mid; low = mid + 1
else:              high = mid - 1
solutions.story: Opposite direction from painter's: maximize on success → go right. Predicate is greedy fit-them-in.
